analysis.one_liner: Requires government and insurers to pay for disability care at home instead of forcing people into institutions.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 202 cosponsors — 199 Democrats and 3 Republicans — but never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for state governments, local governments, and insurers that pay for long-term care to deny disabled people the services they need to live at home — things like help with bathing, meals, medication, and getting around. It would ban waiting lists, cost caps, and other policies that push people into nursing homes, require that people be offered home-based care before being institutionalized, and let individuals sue in federal court to enforce these rights. The bill was referred to two House committees and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: People with disabilities who need help with daily living and would qualify for a nursing home or other institution but want to live in their own homes or in their communities, along with their families and unpaid caregivers. The bill also requires states to make enough affordable, accessible housing available for them to actually choose community living, and requires payment rates adequate to support a home care workforce.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits public entities and long-term care insurers from denying community-based services to disabled people who qualify for institutional placement, including by imposing eligibility criteria, cost caps, or waiting lists.
Requires that people be offered community-based services before institutionalization, and that institutionalized people be regularly notified of community alternatives.

Requires the Justice Department to issue regulations within two years requiring governments and insurers to provide home and community services to anyone who would otherwise qualify for an institution.
Lets individuals sue in federal court for damages and immediate injunctive relief to prevent institutionalization, with possible appointed counsel and attorney's fees.
Requires governments to ensure enough affordable, accessible, integrated housing — not tied to a care provider — and adequate payment rates to support a home care workforce.

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments and insurers that fund long-term care would bear the cost of providing home-based services instead of cheaper-to-cap institutional care; nursing homes and other institutional providers would lose residents and revenue.

drawbacks.text: The bill is a large mandate on states: it requires transition plans with annual targets and timelines — up to 12 years — to shift funding from institutions to community services, but appropriates only $10 million for federal technical assistance, leaving states to find the money.

Private long-term care insurers would face self-evaluations, public hearings, Justice Department enforcement, and civil penalties up to $100,000 for a first violation and $200,000 for subsequent ones, plus damages in individual lawsuits.
Moving care from institutions to homes depends on a scarce paid home care workforce; the bill tries to address this by requiring adequate payment rates, but does not guarantee the workers will exist.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For disabled people stuck on Medicaid waiting lists or placed in nursing homes against their will, the benefit is concrete and life-changing: the choice to live at home with paid help. The costs are real — a large, long-term shift of public money from institutional care to community care — but home-based care is typically cheaper per person than institutional care, and the bill gives states up to a dozen years to adjust. The main design weakness is that the federal government mandates the outcome while leaving most of the funding burden on states.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees, then to their subcommittees, and sat there without a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote until the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Yvette Clarke (D-NY) introduced the bill on February 28, 2022.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health on February 28, 2022, and to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties on November 1, 2022.
No further action was taken: the bill received no committee markup, no floor vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing homes and other institutional care providers keep the current system in which institutional care is guaranteed while home-based care is rationed through waiting lists. State governments avoid new obligations to fund community-based services, and disabled people who wanted out of institutions gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Yvette D. Clarke
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill with 47 original cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and never took it up for a vote.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, sent it to its Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties Subcommittee in November 2022, and never took it up for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: 202 of the bill's 202 supporters in the House were cosponsors: 199 Democrats and 3 Republicans, so backing was heavily but not entirely along party lines; no recorded opposition ever appeared because the bill never came to a vote.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and institutional long-term care providers
industries.note: The bill requires states to shift funding from institutions to home- and community-based care and bans policies that push people into institutions, cutting into the guaranteed institutional revenue stream. Its interest in the current system — institutional care as an entitlement, home care as a rationed extra — runs against what disabled people want.

industries.industry: Home care agencies and care workers
industries.note: Moving people out of institutions and onto home-based services creates demand for home care workers, and the bill requires payment rates adequate to support that workforce, which the bill treats as the key to making community living real.

The bill defines covered insurers broadly, subjects them to self-evaluations, public hearings, Justice Department enforcement, civil penalties of up to $200,000, and individual lawsuits with damages. Insurers currently benefit from cost caps and waiting lists the bill would prohibit.

States would face enforceable transition plans, self-evaluations, and lawsuits, and would bear most of the cost of guaranteeing community-based services. But home-based care is generally less expensive per person than institutional care, so states with large waiting lists could eventually save money.
